Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?

   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Verizon fits Rule Breaker investing poorly: it is a mature telecom carrier in a slow-growing US market, its revenue grew from $128.3 billion in 2020 to just $138.2 billion in 2025, and it is a follower rather than the top dog on speed or growth. It has a well-known brand and a new outside CEO, but no clear sustainable edge that rivals cannot copy.
summaries.buffett: Verizon is simple to understand and sits in a three-player US market with high barriers to entry, which Buffett-style investors value. But its return on capital is ordinary, it carries $165.2 billion of debt, its operating cash flow fell from $41.8 billion in 2020 to $37.1 billion in 2025, and price rises in 2025 drove customers away, so the moat and pricing power are weaker than in his favourite holdings.
summaries.munger: Munger would see an understandable, durable utility-like business at a low multiple (about 11.7 times trailing earnings), but also a capital-hungry, heavily indebted company in a market where three similar rivals compete on price. It is not the kind of high-return, compounding 'great business' he preferred.
summaries.lynch: Verizon fits Lynch's slow-grower or stalwart category: a big, well-known company paying a 6.3% dividend yield while growing revenue around 1-3% a year. Its P/E of about 11.7 is far above its earnings growth rate, so it fails the PEG-style test, though a turnaround story under new CEO Dan Schulman offers some interest.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's growth tests are mostly not met: Verizon's sales have barely grown in five years, R&D-driven new products are few, and margins have not risen. Management's 2026 push on fiber-plus-mobile bundles and cost savings is sensible but is a defensive turnaround rather than long-run product-led growth.
summaries.graham: Verizon passes several of Graham's defensive tests: it is very large, has been profitable every year, has paid dividends for decades, trades at about 12 times its three-year average earnings and has P/E times P/B of about 20.7. It fails on financial strength (current ratio about 0.6 and heavy debt) and on ten-year earnings growth, since 2025 diluted EPS of $4.06 is below 2021's $5.32.
summaries.thiel: Verizon does not fit Thiel's framework: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals, competes in a mature market with AT&T, T-Mobile and cable companies, and offers a largely interchangeable service. Its durable spectrum and network assets give it lasting position, but not monopoly-like economics.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on companies riding big platform shifts with improving growth and efficiency; Verizon is a mature carrier with low growth, though its 2026 cost cuts (about $5 billion of targeted savings) and rising free cash flow fit his 'get fit' theme. AI-related fiber demand is a small tailwind, not a core driver.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings, liquidity tailwinds and catalysts; Verizon has modest guided adjusted EPS growth of 6-7% for 2026 and is sensitive to interest rates through its debt and bond-like dividend. Positive subscriber momentum is a catalyst, but conviction for a concentrated position is unlikely.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital with little debt and strong cash conversion; Verizon converts profit into solid free cash flow ($20.1 billion in 2025) but earns modest returns on a very large, debt-funded asset base. It would likely fail his 'good company' test despite looking cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Verizon offers a reasonable earnings yield (trailing operating income of $28.5 billion is about 8% of its roughly $350 billion enterprise value) but a low return on tangible capital because of its huge network and spectrum assets. It would rank as cheap but not high quality.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented owner-minded managers and strong reinvestment opportunities; Verizon is a decent but not great business, its CEO is a newly hired outsider, and most cash goes to dividends ($11.5 billion in 2025) and debt rather than high-return reinvestment. It fits poorly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary distress bought with low downside; Verizon is simple and recovering from self-inflicted customer losses, and its roughly 10.8% free-cash-flow yield limits downside. But the heavy debt and a crowded, well-followed stock make it a weaker fit for his 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' approach.
summaries.wood: Verizon does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation focus: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing, and its costs do not fall rapidly with scale. It is more likely to be disrupted at the edges (for example by satellite-to-phone service) than to be a disruptor.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and low leverage; Verizon is simple and predictable with large free cash flow, but it is not dominant, has high leverage and limited pricing power. A new CEO-led turnaround could interest an activist, but it only partly fits his criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep sought scale-economies-shared businesses that pass savings to customers and grow stronger over time; Verizon instead raised prices in 2025 and lost customers, and only now promises value-based pricing. Its position in 10-20 years is unlikely to be clearly stronger than today.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and products solving big problems; connectivity is essential, but Verizon's market is mature and its product is hard to tell apart from rivals. It is far from the kind of early-stage, market-creating company Sequoia backs.
summaries.nash: Verizon fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue growth is about 2.5%, debt of $165.2 billion dwarfs $1.8 billion of cash, and it is an old business with no secular-trend tailwind. It is profitable with a 6.3% dividend yield and a cheap forward P/E, but scores only about 40 on his 13-category scorecard and the 12%-discount DCF is well below the price.

momentum.evidence: VZ traded at $44.77 in mid-October 2026, roughly flat versus about $43.91 a year earlier and well below its March 2026 high near $51.68, lagging the broad market.

g4.evidence: New CEO Dan Schulman led PayPal for nine years and holds major board roles, but Verizon has no famous anchor investors beyond typical index and institutional holders (about 62% institutional ownership).

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly call Verizon cheap, not overvalued: it trades at about 8.9 times forward earnings with a 6.3% dividend yield and a consensus Hold rating.

simple.evidence: Verizon sells monthly phone plans, home internet and business connectivity, a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue and dividends have been steady for years, but operating income has been flat ($28.8 billion in 2020, $29.3 billion in 2025) and EPS fell from $5.32 in 2021 to $4.06 in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management candidly admitted in January 2026 that past price rises lacked customer value, but heavy borrowing for spectrum and the Frontier deal, and a CEO change in 2025, show mixed capital discipline.

b6.evidence: The $9.8 billion cash Frontier acquisition (closed January 2026) follows AT&T's fiber strategy, but it fits Verizon's core business rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: With 2025 operating income of $29.3 billion on roughly $245 billion of debt-plus-equity capital, after-tax returns are under 10% and rely heavily on debt.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capex) was $20.1 billion in 2025, above net income attributable to Verizon of $17.2 billion.

b10.evidence: Despite heavy reinvestment in spectrum and networks, the share price fell from about $52 in October 2021 to $44.77 in October 2026 and operating income barely grew.

safety.evidence: At about 9.3 times 2025 free cash flow ($20.1 billion vs a $186.7 billion market value) the stock looks cheap, but $165.2 billion of debt shrinks the margin of safety for shareholders.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 8.9 and a 10.8% free-cash-flow yield are reasonable for a low-growth but stable business.

mu5.evidence: Demand for connectivity is steady, but high leverage, price wars with cable companies and T-Mobile, and refinancing risk are real ways the equity could suffer.

reinvest.evidence: Verizon must spend $16.0-16.5 billion a year on capex just to keep its network competitive, and returns on that spending are modest.

ly2.evidence: Verizon is a classic slow grower/stalwart with a turnaround angle: a new CEO aiming to grow customers through fiber-plus-mobile bundles.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 11.7 is far above the roughly 6-7% guided 2026 adjusted EPS growth.

runway.evidence: Analyst consensus sees revenue rising only to about $149.6 billion by 2030 from $138.2 billion in 2025, about 1.6% a year.

ly7.evidence: Verizon bought back $3.5 billion of stock in the first half of 2026 and diluted shares fell to 4,171 million in Q2 2026, but insiders sold and did not buy in the past three months.

ly8.evidence: Verizon is one of the most widely followed US stocks, covered by about 20 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Verizon has added 5G home internet (6.2 million connections) and is expanding fiber through Frontier, but new products are mostly connectivity variants.

fi3.evidence: Verizon does not report large R&D-driven product breakthroughs, and revenue grew less than 2% a year from 2020 to 2025.

fi4.evidence: Verizon has a large retail and business sales force and returned to +616,000 postpaid phone adds in Q4 2025, but it trailed AT&T (432,000) in Q2 2026 with 184,000.

longterm.evidence: Building fiber via Frontier and moving away from 'empty price increases' are long-term moves, but big job cuts and buybacks show strong short-term cost focus.

gr1.evidence: Verizon had $138.2 billion of 2025 revenue and a market value around $187 billion.

ni10.evidence: Verizon reported positive net income in each year, including $11.6 billion attributable even in 2023 after a $5.8 billion goodwill impairment.

gr4.evidence: Verizon has paid a quarterly dividend every year since its formation in 2000 and declared 70.75 cents per share in September 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS was $4.06 in 2025, below $4.30 in 2020 and $5.32 in 2021, so it has not grown by a third.

gr6.evidence: The price of $44.77 is about 12.3 times the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of $3.65.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 11.7 times P/B of about 1.8 gives about 20.7, under 22.5.

th1.evidence: Verizon's network is comparable to AT&T's and T-Mobile's; RootMetrics scored it 98.4 vs AT&T's 98.3 in 1H 2026.

timing.evidence: Demand for fiber and connectivity for AI data centers is growing, but the core wireless market is mature.

th3.evidence: Verizon started as a large regional Bell company, not as the leader of a small niche.

team.evidence: CEO Dan Schulman has a strong record from PayPal, but he took over only in October 2025 and the team is still being reshaped.

th5.evidence: Verizon has a national retail store network, online sales and a business sales force reaching millions of customers.

durable.evidence: Spectrum licences and a dense fiber network should keep Verizon a top US carrier, but satellite-to-phone and cable MVNOs could erode its share.

th7.evidence: Its fiber-plus-mobile convergence strategy is the same one AT&T, T-Mobile and cable companies already pursue.

trend.evidence: Verizon cites 'the emergence of AI infrastructure revenue' as a growth driver, but AI is a small part of its business.

dr1.evidence: Verizon raised 2026 guidance in July to adjusted EPS of $4.99-5.04 (6-7% growth), but GAAP Q2 2026 EPS fell to $0.92 from $1.18.

dr2.evidence: Lower churn, Frontier bundles and $5 billion of targeted cost savings could improve results, but much of this is already expected.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would help a company with $165.2 billion of debt and quarterly interest expense near $2 billion, but higher rates would hurt.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on October 26, 2026, Frontier integration synergies and buybacks of up to $4.5 billion in 2026 are possible catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Slow growth, high leverage and intense competition make a high-conviction concentrated position hard to justify.

gm.evidence: Revenue minus cost of services and equipment gave a gross margin of about 58.9% in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $20.1 billion is about 10.8% of the roughly $186.7 billion market value.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $28.5 billion is about 8.1% of an enterprise value near $350 billion.

pa2.evidence: Customer losses from 2025 price rises were partly self-inflicted and are reversing (+184,000 postpaid phone adds in Q2 2026), but competition from cable is structural.

pa4.evidence: Stable cash flow makes collapse unlikely, but leverage of about $165 billion means a permanent loss of some equity value is possible.

wo1.evidence: Verizon is a telecom carrier, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Network costs do not fall quickly with volume; capex stays at $16-17 billion a year.

wo3.evidence: Verizon does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow only about 1.6% a year through 2030.

ac3.evidence: With $165.2 billion of debt and interest expense of $3.9 billion in the first half of 2026, Verizon is sensitive to interest rates.

ns1.evidence: Verizon raised prices several times in 2025 instead of passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Rivals T-Mobile and cable companies are gaining share, so Verizon's position in 10-20 years is not clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: Reliable mobile and home internet are essential for nearly every household and business.

tn1.evidence: Verizon is an old telecom business retrofitting toward AI fiber demand, not a company built for a new secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Verizon as a slow-growth telecom carrier, which matches what it is becoming.

tn3.evidence: Verizon is a large-cap US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Verizon is profitable and revenue grew in 2024 and 2025, but it fell in 2023 and debt of $165.2 billion far exceeds cash of $1.8 billion.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive ($10.2 billion in H1 2026), but debt exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 2.5% in 2025 and fell 0.7% year over year in Q2 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 2.5% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 14.6% gives about 17, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 2.5% while total operating expenses grew 2.7% ($106.1 billion to $108.9 billion).

tn9.evidence: Debt far exceeds cash and operating margin was about 20.5% over the last twelve months, near the line, while revenue growth is well under 10%.

tn10.evidence: Verizon faces ongoing FCC regulation and spectrum policy risk but no major existential legal threat.

tn11.evidence: Verizon provides mobile and home internet connectivity that helps households and businesses stay connected, charging monthly subscriptions; customers choose it mainly for coverage and reliability.

tn13.evidence: About 40: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin (about 20.5%) 5, short interest (2.14%) 10, institutional ownership (62%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 0, talent 5.

tn20.evidence: Verizon beat Q2 2026 adjusted EPS consensus ($1.30 vs $1.27), but its revenue fell 0.7% year over year.

tn21.evidence: No fraud or auditor change (Ernst & Young remains auditor), but margins have not expanded and Verizon bought Frontier for about $9.8 billion cash plus $12.9 billion of assumed debt.

tn22.evidence: Verizon has $138.2 billion of revenue, steady profits, buys back rather than sells shares, and attracts little hype.

tn25.evidence: With about 0.3% average growth and a 14.4% FCF margin, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth give equity value of roughly $14 per share after $163 billion of net debt, far below $44.77.
